paper.title_en: A fast radio burst from a non-targeted low-frequency survey
paper.abstract_en: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are bright, millisecond-duration transient radio signals of extragalactic origin with unknown source and emission mechanisms. While several thousand FRBs have been discovered at frequencies above 400 MHz, detections at lower frequencies have been exceptionally rare. Contributing to their rarity are the magnified dispersive delay, in the tens of seconds, and signal scattering that make low-frequency searches with established techniques computationally prohibitive. In particular, the only confirmed detection below 300 MHz came from a Low-Frequency Array observing campaign targeted at FRB 20180916B, a source already known to emit at higher frequencies. Here we present the first non-targeted detection of an FRB below 300 MHz, achieved in a wide-field, imaging-based survey with the Murchison Widefield Array. The implied FRB rate is consistent with that observed at higher frequencies, demonstrating that non-targeted wide-field surveys can uncover an unbiased, large low-frequency FRB population. This result challenges models invoking severe scattering or absorption to explain previous non-detections, and strengthens the case of low-frequency observations as promising avenue to study the local environment of FRBs.
